title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: Containers
summary: A container is a lightweight, OS-level virtualization that packages an application with its dependencies into a portable unit, sharing the host kernel while isolating its processes, filesystem, and network namespace — enabling…
objectives: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine, and why does it matter?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A container is a lightweight, OS-level virtualization that packages an application with its dependencies into a portable unit, sharing the host kernel while isolating its processes, filesystem, and network namespace — enabling sub-second startup and consistent execution across environments.
Containers are the operational primitive that made the modern microservices boom possible, and they emerged from a lineage of operating-system features rather than from hypervisor technology. Where a virtual machine virtualizes the hardware (the hypervisor emulates a CPU, NIC, and disk for each guest), a container virtualizes the operating system itself — multiple containers share a single Linux kernel but each sees its own process tree, filesystem, network interfaces, and user IDs. The enabling primitives — namespaces for isolation and cgroups for resource limits — were added to the Linux kernel between 2002 and 2013. LXC, OpenVZ, and Solaris Zones were early products that exposed these primitives, but it was Docker, released in 2013, that gave the world a usable packaging format, a build tool, and a registry, igniting the container revolution. Today Docker, containerd, CRI-O, and the broader OCI (Open Container Initiative) ecosystem run essentially every modern stateless workload, and Google has stated that essentially every Google service runs in a container — they have been doing it internally since 2004 with Borg, long before Docker existed.

The defining property of a container is layered imaging. A container image is not a single monolithic file; it is a stack of read-only layers, each representing the result of one instruction in a Dockerfile. A base layer might be `ubuntu:22.04`, the next adds `apt install python3`, the next copies the application code, the next sets the entrypoint. Each layer is content-addressed by SHA, so identical layers across images are stored once and pulled once. When a container runs, the runtime stacks the image layers read-only and adds a thin writable layer on top for the container's runtime modifications. This design has three huge consequences: builds are cacheable (a code change only invalidates the layers above it), distribution is efficient (a 1000-instance fleet shares the same base layer), and images are reproducible (the same SHA is the same bytes everywhere). Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, and the OCI registries all exploit this layering for fast distribution.

The second property is sub-second startup. A VM takes 30–60 seconds to boot because it must initialize a kernel, mount filesystems, and start init services. A container takes 50–500 milliseconds to start because it is just a process fork on the host kernel — no kernel boot, no init system, no BIOS. This is the property that enables Kubernetes autoscaling, AWS Fargate, and serverless containers like Cloud Run. When a Cloud Run service scales from zero to a thousand instances in response to a traffic spike, it is the container's sub-second startup that makes it feasible. Netflix's Titus container platform, launched in 2017, replaced many of their EC2-based workloads precisely because containers scaled faster than VMs and packed more densely, reducing cost and improving latency for video-encoding workers.

The third property is portability. A container image that builds and runs on a developer's Mac will run identically on an EC2 instance, a GCP Compute Engine VM, an on-prem Kubernetes cluster, or a managed serverless platform — as long as the host kernel is compatible (Linux containers need a Linux kernel; Mac and Windows run them in a lightweight VM). This is the "build once, run anywhere" promise, and it is largely true in practice for stateless applications. The caveats are kernel version mismatches (an image built with newer syscalls may fail on older kernels) and CPU architecture differences (an x86 image will not run on ARM without emulation or rebuild), but for most workloads portability is real. Spotify's migration to Docker in 2014–2016 eliminated an entire class of "works on my machine" bugs that had plagued their deployment pipeline.

The fourth property is density. Because containers share the host kernel and do not run a full guest OS, dozens or hundreds of containers can run on a single host. A typical EC2 m5.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32GB RAM) might run 3–4 VMs comfortably or 30–50 containers depending on their resource footprint. This density advantage is the economic argument for containers — you pack more workloads onto fewer hosts, reducing infrastructure cost. Google's Borg system, the internal predecessor to Kubernetes, regularly runs 10,000+ containers per host on large machines, an extreme that public clouds do not reach but that illustrates the density ceiling. The trade-off is that containers offer weaker isolation than VMs — a container escape (a kernel exploit that lets a container process break into the host) compromises every container on the host, while a VM escape is far rarer. This is why security-sensitive workloads like multi-tenant SaaS often run containers inside VMs (AWS Firecracker, Google gVisor) for defense in depth.

The fifth property is the orchestration dependency. A single container is trivial to run with `docker run`. A fleet of thousands of containers across hundreds of hosts requires an orchestrator — Kubernetes, Amazon ECS, Docker Swarm, HashiCorp Nomad — to schedule containers onto hosts, restart them on failure, scale them with load, and roll out new versions. Kubernetes won the orchestrator war by 2018 and is now the de facto standard. The trade-off is that Kubernetes introduces enormous operational complexity — a typical production cluster requires RBAC, networking (CNI), storage (CSI), ingress controllers, service mesh, logging, monitoring, and dedicated SREs to operate. This complexity is what drove the rise of managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) and PaaS-on-Kubernetes abstractions (Render, Fly.io, Cloud Run), which trade flexibility for reduced operational burden.

The real-world impact is hard to overstate. Netflix's Titus runs most of their streaming and encoding workloads. Spotify migrated from EC2 AMIs to Docker for deployment consistency. Every major cloud runs serverless containers (AWS Fargate, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps) that hide the orchestrator entirely while preserving the container packaging format. The trajectory is clear: containers have become the universal deployment unit for stateless applications, with VMs persisting for stateful workloads and specialized use cases (databases, GPU ML training), and serverless functions persisting for event-driven workloads. The trade-off summary: containers offer portability, density, and fast startup at the cost of weaker isolation than VMs and the operational complexity of orchestration.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Host["Host OS (Linux Kernel)"] subgraph Container1["Container A"] A1[App A] --- A2[libs A] --- A3[fs layer 1+2+3] end subgraph Container2["Container B"] B1[App B] --- B2[libs B] --- B3[fs layer 1+4+5] end subgraph Container3["Container C"] C1[App C] --- C2[libs C] --- C3[fs layer 1+6+7] end Kernel[Shared Kernel
namespaces + cgroups] Container1 --> Kernel Container2 --> Kernel Container3 --> Kernel end Registry[Container Registry
Docker Hub / ECR / GCR] -.->|pull layers| Container1 Registry -.->|pull layers| Container2 Registry -.->|pull layers| Container3 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------------------------------------------------------+ | Host (Linux kernel: namespaces + cgroups) | | | | +-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+ | | | Container A | | Container B | | Container C | | | | nginx | | python app | | redis | | | | pid ns | | pid ns | | pid ns | | | | net ns | | net ns | | net ns | | | | mnt ns | | mnt ns | | mnt ns | | | +-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+ | | | | | | | v v v | | +------------------------------------------------+ | | | Shared kernel (syscalls, TCP/IP, scheduler) | | | +------------------------------------------------+ | | | | cgroups limit: CPU 1core | 2core | 0.5core | | RAM 1GB | 4GB | 512MB | +-----------------------------------------------------------+ Image layers (content-addressed, shared): layer 1 (ubuntu:22.04) <-- shared by A, B, C layer 2 (apt python3) <-- shared by B, C layer 3 (COPY app.py) <-- only A layer 4 (COPY app.py) <-- only B ... ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A container image is built as a stack of read-only layers, each content-addressed by SHA; identical layers across images are stored once in the registry and pulled once per host. 2. At run time, the container runtime (Docker, containerd) calls the kernel to create namespaces (pid, net, mnt, user) and a cgroup for resource limits, then forks a process inside them that sees only its own filesystem and process tree. 3. Because the container is just a host process with namespace isolation, startup is a fork — milliseconds, not the seconds a VM needs to boot a kernel. 4. An orchestrator (Kubernetes, ECS) schedules containers across hosts based on resource requests, restarts them on failure, and rolls out new versions by replacing containers atomically.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Mimics Docker Hub / ECR / GCR: content-addressed layer store.
- Mimics Docker / containerd / CRI-O: build, run, stop containers.
- dockerfile: list of (cmd, content_bytes, size_mb).
- Tiny orchestrator: place containers across hosts based on resources.
- Container_runtime.py - runnable mock of a container runtime.
- Models: layered image build, registry pull with layer sharing,
- Container run/stop, cgroup limits, and a tiny scheduler.
- Content-addressed dedup: same digest = same bytes, stored once

**Defines:** `Layer`, `Image`, `Container`, `Registry`, `ContainerRuntime`, `Scheduler`

```python
# container_runtime.py - runnable mock of a container runtime.
# Models: layered image build, registry pull with layer sharing,
# container run/stop, cgroup limits, and a tiny scheduler.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Dict, Optional, Set
import uuid, time, hashlib

@dataclass
class Layer:
    digest: str            # sha256 of content
    cmd: str               # dockerfile instruction that produced it
    size_mb: int

@dataclass
class Image:
    name: str
    tag: str
    layers: List[Layer] = field(default_factory=list)
    entrypoint: str = "sh"

    @property
    def ref(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name}:{self.tag}"

@dataclass
class Container:
    container_id: str
    image_ref: str
    name: str
    state: str = "created"     # created -> running -> stopped -> exited
    pid: Optional[int] = None
    cpu_limit: float = 1.0     # cores
    mem_limit_mb: int = 512
    started_at: Optional[float] = None

class Registry:
    """Mimics Docker Hub / ECR / GCR: content-addressed layer store."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.images: Dict[str, Image] = {}
        self.layers: Dict[str, Layer] = {}    # digest -> layer (deduped)

    def push(self, image: Image):
        for layer in image.layers:
            # Content-addressed dedup: same digest = same bytes, stored once
            if layer.digest not in self.layers:
                self.layers[layer.digest] = layer
                print(f"[registry] stored new layer {layer.digest[:12]} ({layer.size_mb}MB)")
            else:
                print(f"[registry] layer {layer.digest[:12]} already present (dedup)")
        self.images[image.ref] = image
        print(f"[registry] pushed {image.ref} ({len(image.layers)} layers)")

    def pull(self, ref: str) -> Image:
        img = self.images[ref]
        print(f"[registry] pulling {ref} ({len(img.layers)} layers)")
        return img

class ContainerRuntime:
    """Mimics Docker / containerd / CRI-O: build, run, stop containers."""
    def __init__(self, host_id: str):
        self.host_id = host_id
        self.containers: Dict[str, Container] = {}
        self.local_layers: Set[str] = set()   # layers already pulled on host

    def build(self, name: str, tag: str, dockerfile: List[tuple]) -> Image:
        """dockerfile: list of (cmd, content_bytes, size_mb). Returns Image."""
        img = Image(name, tag)
        prev_digest = ""
        for cmd, content, size in dockerfile:
            # Content-addressed: digest depends on content + parent
            h = hashlib.sha256((prev_digest + cmd + content).encode()).hexdigest()
            layer = Layer(digest=h, cmd=cmd, size_mb=size)
            img.layers.append(layer)
            prev_digest = h
            print(f"[build] layer: {cmd[:40]:40s} -> {h[:12]} ({size}MB)")
        img.entrypoint = "/app/start.sh"
        print(f"[build] image {img.ref} built, {len(img.layers)} layers")
        return img

    def run(self, image: Image, name: str,
            cpu: float = 1.0, mem: int = 512) -> Container:
        # Pull missing layers (deduped)
        for layer in image.layers:
            if layer.digest not in self.local_layers:
                print(f"[run] pulling layer {layer.digest[:12]} ({layer.size_mb}MB)")
                self.local_layers.add(layer.digest)
            else:
                print(f"[run] layer {layer.digest[:12]} cached locally")
        cid = "c-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
        c = Container(cid, image.ref, name,
                      cpu_limit=cpu, mem_limit_mb=mem)
        self.containers[cid] = c
        # Kernel namespace + cgroup creation = milliseconds
        c.state = "running"
        c.pid = abs(hash(cid)) % 30000 + 1000
        c.started_at = time.time()
        print(f"[run] container {cid} (pid={c.pid}) running, "
              f"cpu={cpu}c mem={mem}MB img={image.ref}")
        return c

    def stop(self, cid: str):
        c = self.containers.get(cid)
        if c and c.state == "running":
            uptime = time.time() - c.started_at
            c.state = "stopped"
            print(f"[stop] {cid} stopped after {uptime:.2f}s, "
                  f"writable layer discarded")

    def ps(self) -> List[Container]:
        return [c for c in self.containers.values() if c.state == "running"]

class Scheduler:
    """Tiny orchestrator: place containers across hosts based on resources."""
    def __init__(self, hosts: List[ContainerRuntime]):
        self.hosts = hosts

    def schedule(self, image: Image, name: str,
                 cpu: float, mem: int) -> Container:
        # Pick the host with most free capacity (Bin-packing by cpu)
        target = min(self.hosts,
                     key=lambda h: sum(c.cpu_limit for c in h.ps()))
        print(f"[sched] placed '{name}' on host {target.host_id}")
        return target.run(image, name, cpu, mem)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    reg = Registry()
    rt = ContainerRuntime("host-1")

    # Build a python web image
    dockerfile = [
        ("FROM ubuntu:22.04",       "base",      80),
        ("RUN apt install python3", "python",    60),
        ("COPY app.py /app/",       "code-v1",    2),
        ("CMD /app/start.sh",       "cmd",        0),
    ]
    img = rt.build("myapp", "v1", dockerfile)
    reg.push(img)

    # Run 3 instances - layers cached locally after first
    c1 = rt.run(img, "web-1", cpu=0.5, mem=256)
    c2 = rt.run(img, "web-2", cpu=0.5, mem=256)
    c3 = rt.run(img, "worker-1", cpu=1.0, mem=512)

    print(f"\nrunning containers: {len(rt.ps())}")
    rt.stop(c1.container_id)
    print(f"running after stop: {len(rt.ps())}")

    # Scheduler across multiple hosts
    print("\n--- scheduler demo ---")
    hosts = [ContainerRuntime(f"host-{i}") for i in range(1, 4)]
    sched = Scheduler(hosts)
    for i in range(6):
        sched.schedule(img, f"web-{i}", cpu=0.5, mem=256)
```

quiz.question: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine, and why does it matter?
options: Namespaces and cgroups are the two Linux kernel features that make containers possible.
A container escape is a security exploit where a malicious process inside a container breaks out of its namespace isolation and accesses the host kernel or other containers.
The OCI is a Linux Foundation project, formed in 2015 under the Docker-led governance, that defines open standards for container formats and runtimes.
VMs are gigabytes in size (full OS) versus containers in megabytes (just the app and its libs).
quiz.explanation: A virtual machine virtualizes the hardware: the hypervisor presents a fake CPU, NIC, and disk to each guest, and each guest runs its own full kernel, init system, and user space. A container virtualizes the operating system: multiple containers share a single host kernel but each sees its own process tree, filesystem, and network via Linux namespaces, with resource limits enforced by cgroups.

quiz.explanation: Namespaces and cgroups are the two Linux kernel features that make containers possible. Namespaces provide isolation: they give a process a view of system resources that appears to be its own. The pid namespace gives the process its own process IDs (it sees itself as PID 1).

options: VMs are gigabytes in size (full OS) versus containers in megabytes (just the app and its libs).

quiz.explanation: The OCI is a Linux Foundation project, formed in 2015 under the Docker-led governance, that defines open standards for container formats and runtimes. It has two specifications. The OCI Image Spec defines the on-disk format of a container image (manifest, config, layers) so any tool can build images consumable by any runtime.

quiz.question: Why is container orchestration necessary, and what problem does Kubernetes solve?
options: OOMKilled means the kernel killed a container process because it exceeded its cgroup memory limit, which in Kubernetes is containers[].resources.limits.memory.
Docker is the original container product: a monolithic daemon (dockerd) that builds images, runs containers, manages networks and volumes, and exposes a REST API.
Image bloat and slow builds have well-known causes and cures.
A single container is trivial — docker run and you are done.
quiz.explanation: A single container is trivial — docker run and you are done. A production fleet of thousands of containers across hundreds of hosts is intractable without an orchestrator.
